title: Morphy's rook sacrifice against Bird
summary: London, 1858: Henry Bird castles long, and Morphy gives up a rook so his queen can land next to the white king.

steps.title: London, 1858
steps.text: Before Paris, Morphy spent the summer of 1858 in London, playing England's best. Henry Bird was a strong English master who loved unusual openings; an opening that starts by pushing the f-pawn two squares is still called Bird's Opening. Here Bird has White, and Morphy meets 1.e4 with an aggressive early ...f5. You play Black, as Morphy.
steps.narration: London, 1858. Morphy takes on Henry Bird, an English master who loved surprises. This time the surprise comes from Morphy. You play Black.

steps.title: Bird – Morphy, London 1858
steps.text: The game gets sharp early. Bird castles queenside, and his king looks safe behind its pawns. Morphy gives up a rook to get his queen next to it. The game stops at Morphy's key moves.
steps.narration: Bird castles on the queenside and his king looks safe. Watch how Morphy reaches it anyway, and find his key moves.

notes.text: 3...f5: Morphy strikes at the center at once. It is risky, and it makes the game sharp from the start.
12...Qxh5: after a short skirmish on the kingside, Morphy is a pawn up.
15...bxc6: taking back this way opens the b-file for a black rook.
16...Rb8: the rook takes the open file and points at b2.
17.O-O-O: Bird castles queenside. His king sits behind three pawns on a2, b2 and c2.
17...Rxf2!? Morphy gives up a rook on f2 to drag the bishop away from e3. Modern engines prefer a quieter move here, but watch what the bishop stops guarding.
18.Bxf2: Bird takes the rook. Morphy is a whole rook down, but not for long.
20...Qa1+: the queen checks from the corner, and the white king has to walk.
23...Rxb4+: the b-file is open, and the rook joins with check.
26...Bf5+: the last black piece joins the attack with check.
29...Qb1+: the queen will take the rook on h1 next. Bird resigned.

guesses.prompt: Bird's bishop took your rook on f2. Now find the queen move that explains the sacrifice.
guesses.hint: The bishop has left e3. Which square right next to the white king is now unguarded?
guesses.why: 18...Qa3!! The queen lands next to the white king. If the b-pawn takes the queen, the bishop takes back on a3 and it is checkmate. Bird had to play 19.c3, and the queen took on a2 instead.

guesses.prompt: The white king has run to b2. Throw in another piece to open the b-file.
guesses.hint: Your bishop on d6 can capture a pawn standing on the b-file.
guesses.why: 22...Bxb4! If the c-pawn takes back, the b-file opens and the rook on b8 joins the attack with check.

guesses.prompt: The queens are still on, and White's king is out in the open. Find the pawn move that lets your last piece join with check.
guesses.hint: Your bishop wants to check from f5, but your own pawn on e4 blocks that diagonal.
guesses.why: 25...e3! The pawn gets out of the way, so the bishop can check from f5 along the long diagonal. Bird took the pawn, and 26...Bf5+ followed.

steps.title: What does the defender leave behind?
steps.text: Morphy's rook sacrifice had one job: pull the bishop away from e3 so the queen could land on a3. Before you sacrifice, ask what the capturing piece stops guarding when it takes. Here a single bishop was holding the white king together.
steps.narration: The rook sacrifice pulled the bishop away from e3, and that let the queen land on a3. Always ask what a defender stops guarding when it captures.

steps.title: The point of the sacrifice
steps.question: What was the point of Morphy's 17...Rxf2?

options.text: To pull the bishop off e3 so the black queen could reach a3
options.why: Exactly. Once the bishop took on f2, a3 was unguarded and the queen jumped in next to the king.

options.text: To win the f2 pawn for free
options.why: It was not free: Bird took the rook. The pawn was not the point.

options.text: To trade rooks and head for an endgame
options.why: No rooks were traded. Morphy gave up his rook to attack the king.

steps.narration: Last question: what was the rook sacrifice really for?
